speaker: Tony Burke
claim: Net overseas migration has fallen to 292,000 in the year to March 2026, 47% below its post-Covid peak
what_the_data_shows: ABS: net overseas migration was 292,137 in the year to March 2026, 47% below the peak of 555,798 in the year to September 2023.
claim_source: Migration reform to end rorts and bring in the skills Australia needs for a strong economy (media release)

speaker: Tony Burke
claim: The new changes are designed to bring net overseas migration to 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 in 2027-28
what_the_data_shows: The first ABS figures for 2026-27 (the September quarter 2026) are due in March 2027. For context: NOM was 292,137 in the year to March 2026, and 244,235 in the first 9 months of 2025-26. Treasury's May 2026 Budget forecast for 2025-26 is 295,000.
caveats: A forecast, not law; the government says its measures are designed to deliver it
claim_source: Migration reform to end rorts and bring in the skills Australia needs for a strong economy (media release)

speaker: Tanya Plibersek
claim: The government has tripled the number of skilled visas going to people who work in construction
what_the_data_shows: Home Affairs: temporary skilled visas granted to main applicants in building and construction jobs rose from 1,546 in 2021-22, the year Labor took office, to 5,045 in 2025-26: 3.3 times as many. The starting year was a pandemic low; in 2018-19 there were 2,781.
caveats: Temporary skilled visas only (subclass 482, 457 and Skills in Demand); permanent skilled visas are not in this count. 'Construction' is our Building and construction sector
claim_source: 'Race to the bottom': One Nation migration plan slammed (AAP)

speaker: Jim Chalmers
claim: Net overseas migration has nearly halved from its peak and is falling faster than forecast
what_the_data_shows: NOM is down 47% from its peak, close to half. The latest 12 months (292,137) are a little below the May 2026 Budget forecast for 2025-26 (295,000), but above the December 2025 forecast (260,000) that it replaced.
caveats: 2025-26 is not finished; the full-year figure is due in December 2026
claim_source: Migration: 17 Sep 2026: House debates (Hansard, Question Time, via OpenAustralia)

speaker: Angus Taylor
claim: Since Labor was elected, a record 1.4 million people have come in through migration, about 80% of population growth
what_the_data_shows: ABS: NOM added 1,434,149 people from the June quarter 2022 to the September quarter 2025, the latest data when he spoke. That is 80% of population growth (1,799,129). The highest total for any earlier 14 quarters was 917,101. The period began as the borders reopened after Covid, when many students and workers returned.
caveats: Counted from the June quarter 2022, when Labor took office (23 May 2022)
claim_source: Budget Address in Reply (Liberal Party transcript)

speaker: Angus Taylor
claim: Under Labor, Australia has had the worst fall in living standards of any developed country
what_the_data_shows: Testing it needs: OECD comparisons of real household disposable income per person (we hold GDP per person for four countries only).
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: Budget Address in Reply (Liberal Party transcript)

speaker: Andrew Bragg
claim: About 1.5 million people have come into Australia under Labor, against about 500,000 new homes
what_the_data_shows: People: ABS NOM was 1,490,281 from the June quarter 2022 to the December quarter 2025, close to 1.5 million. Homes: the ABS counts 665,890 homes completed over the same period, 33% more than 500,000. Counting births minus deaths too, the population grew by 1,877,286, or 2.8 people per home completed; the average household is 2.5 people (Census 2021).
caveats: Completions are gross: homes knocked down are not subtracted
claim_source: Migration: 16 Sep 2026: Senate debates (Hansard, via OpenAustralia)

speaker: Angus Taylor and Jonathon Duniam
claim: Net permanent and long-term arrivals were 479,000 in the year to February 2026, and have run at 400,000 to 500,000 a year under Labor
what_the_data_shows: This figure uses a different measure (intended stays). NOM, the official measure of how many people stay, was 292,137 in the year to March 2026. Testing it needs: ABS Overseas Arrivals and Departures (permanent and long-term movements), which counts intended stays.
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: Migration numbers explode under Labor as standards slip (Liberal Party release)

speaker: Pauline Hanson
claim: Labor has added 1.6 million people to Australia's population since taking office in 2022
what_the_data_shows: Migration added 1,490,281 people from the June quarter 2022 to the December quarter 2025 (the latest data when she spoke) and 1,591,286 to March 2026. Counting births minus deaths too, the population grew by 2,008,173 over that time. So 1.6 million is about right for migration alone, and short of total growth.
caveats: The claim does not say whether it means migration or all population growth
claim_source: Migration: 16 Sep 2026: Senate debates (Hansard, via OpenAustralia)

speaker: Pauline Hanson
claim: Since taking office, Labor has repeatedly overshot its own net migration forecasts
what_the_data_shows: Each year's outcome came in above the government's first Budget forecast for it. 2022-23: 538,341 against 235,000 (October 2022 Budget); 2023-24: 429,162 against 315,000 (May 2023 Budget); 2024-25: 301,572 against 260,000 (May 2024 Budget). The gap has narrowed each year.
caveats: The forecasts are Treasury's. The 2022-23 gap came as international borders reopened
claim_source: Social media post, as reported by ABC News: Hanson intervenes after One Nation MP says migration plan 'not too different' to Labor

speaker: Sean Bell
claim: Almost four in five temporary residents live in capital cities, half of them in Sydney and Melbourne
what_the_data_shows: Testing it needs: ABS 'Temporary visa holders in Australia' (Census-linked), by capital city.
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: Migration: 16 Sep 2026: Senate debates (Hansard, via OpenAustralia)

speaker: One Nation (party)
claim: A One Nation government would cut temporary visas by 750,000, giving net negative migration for three years, then cap net migration at 130,000 a year
what_the_data_shows: Home Affairs counted 2,878,973 temporary visa holders on 31 August 2026, so 750,000 is about 26% of them. If all 766,000 in the party's own breakdown left over three years, about 255,333 more people would leave than arrive each year. The lowest year since the First World War was 2020-21, with the borders closed, when 84,935 more people left than arrived.
caveats: Temporary visa holders include visitors and New Zealanders on Special Category visas, who are not in the party's targeted groups
claim_source: One Nation's Immigration Plan: Cut 750,000 Temporary Visas and Cap Migration

speaker: David Shoebridge
claim: Twice as many people are on bridging visas now as three years ago, which he attributes to Labor policy
what_the_data_shows: Home Affairs: 440,571 people held bridging visas on 31 August 2026, against 191,235 on 30 September 2023: 2.3 times as many, so more than double. The data does not show why; his explanation is not tested here.
caveats: Bridging visas cover people waiting on a decision, including appeals and onshore applications
claim_source: Labor's migration policy a bumbling return to Abbott era (Greens media release)

speaker: Australian Greens (party)
claim: Partner visa waiting times have doubled in recent years to 40 months, and parent visas now take 30 years
what_the_data_shows: Testing it needs: Home Affairs processing times by visa subclass over several years (its online tool shows only current times).
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: Labor's migration policy a bumbling return to Abbott era (Greens media release)

speaker: Melissa Byrne (Master Builders Australia)
claim: About 7,040 skilled visa holders were working in core construction trades as at September 2025
what_the_data_shows: Home Affairs: 6,594 main applicants on temporary skilled visas were in construction and electrical trades at 30 September 2025, close to 7,040 (their list of core trades may differ a little). That is about 11 for every 1,000 people working in those trades.
caveats: Our count covers ANZSCO construction trades (33) and electricians (341)
claim_source: Opening Statement: Inquiry into the value of skilled migration to Australia (Master Builders)

speaker: Luke Sheehy (Universities Australia)
claim: International students make up about 6% of Australia's rental market
what_the_data_shows: Testing it needs: ABS Census housing tenure for temporary visa holders, and the study the release cites.
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: International students not low-hanging fruit in race to the bottom (media release)

speaker: Andrew McKellar (ACCI)
claim: Major cuts to skilled migration would damage the economy, hit the federal budget and weaken the capacity to provide services and lift living standards
what_the_data_shows: Published estimates back the budget point: Treasury (2021) put each skilled primary applicant's lifetime contribution at about $415,000 (net present value, 2018-19 dollars). The 2026 Intergenerational Report, as reported, found that 185,000 a year instead of 235,000 leaves GDP per person only about $400 lower by 2065-66, with gross debt about 4.8 points of GDP higher. So the budget effect is clear; the effect on living standards per person is small.
caveats: Other researchers' estimates under their own assumptions. Check the IGR figures against its Appendix A4
claim_source: 'Race to the bottom': One Nation migration plan slammed (AAP)

speaker: Australian Workers' Union
claim: Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) workers make up about 6% of agricultural workers and nearly a third of meat processing workers
what_the_data_shows: Testing it needs: Department of Employment PALM scheme data by industry, against ABS Labour Force employment.
caveats: Not a judgement on the claim
claim_source: Government must not miss PALM reform opportunity: AWU (media release)

speaker: ACTU
claim: Some employers game the system, using temporary migration as cheap labour instead of training local workers
what_the_data_shows: Counts can't show why employers sponsor visas or whether visas replace training. For scale, temporary skilled visa grants to main applicants (2025-26) and apprentice and trainee completions (year to March 2026) were: hospitality and food: 9,456 visas against 5,440 completions; building and construction: 5,045 visas against 32,235 completions; mechanics and metal trades: 7,750 visas against 15,105 completions.
caveats: Testing the claim would need employer-level data on sponsorship and training
claim_source: Inquiry into the Value of Skilled Migration to Australia (ACTU submission)
